The Report 


of the 


General Secretary 


ow 


Young Men’s Christian Association 
of Greater Montreal 


Cow 


For the Year Ending March 31st, 1929 


ow 


In recording the progress and achieve- 
ments of the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal in its 
78th year of service, it is desirable to avoid 
the use of superlatives, yet it will not be 
easy to find another year since the Associa- 
tion was first organized when so many 
matters of large importance to the youth of | 
our city are to be recorded. 


At the head of the achievements stands 


: % J. W. Beaton 
President the carrying through in the first month of | General Secretary 


GeRraLp W. Birks 


”M.C.A. ° Montreal Y.M.C.. 
Montreal Y.M-C-A. our fiscal year of the public phase of our “0”! %--G-A 


Expansion Campaign Fund for $1,500,000.00, the need for which was 
announced at our 75th Anniversary Dinner nearly four years ago. The 
splendid response of our citizens both as workers in the campaign and in 
their financial backing of this large venture in faith was most inspiring. 
This was the largest campaign ever carried through by any Association in 
Canada, and it has focussed unusual attention upon our work with the 
result that we have since been called upon to release for National and 
International service some of our ablest laymen and secretaries. 


The year has been an extremely active one in all fields of service and 
activity. The doors of our nine Branches and evening College have been 
wide open to the boys and young men resident in Greater Montreal, and 
to the thousands of young men who came to our city as strangers. We 
have made new enrolment records in number of members, campers and 
students in our evening College. The Y.M.C.A. is a definitely and 
avowedly Christian organization and bases its ideals on the life and 
teachings of Jesus Christ, believing that investments in equipment for 
physical, social, educational and religious work are even more significant 
than hospitals, asylums and jails. We have sought to unite in our fellow- 
ship those men and boys of all classes and creeds who are in sympathy 
with our purpose, and who desire to work for its accomplishment, 


Il 


On this basis, we have confidently claimed the sympathy and support 
of all men of good will who realize the supreme importance of teaching 
ideals to the youth of our day and generation. 


Finance and Property: 


At the close of our Expansion Campaign for $1,500,- 

$1,500,000 Expan- (00.00, held last April, definite pledges and cash had been 

sion Campaign received totalling $1,300,000.10, of which $50,000.00 was 

Fund conditional upon the full objective being reached. To 

that amount our President, Mr. Gerald W. Birks, and 

Mr. T. B. Macaulay have since added generous conditional gifts of $25,000 

and $5,000.00 respectively, which with contributions secured in the 

interim leaves us within $140,000.00 of our goal. Every effort is 

being maintained to secure the balance of the money required in order 
that the full development programme may be carried through. 


An amount of $110,000.00 was included 
in the Expansion Campaign budget for the 
current operations of the Association for 
the past year and in spite of the inability 
of the Central, North, St. Paul, Verdun and 
MountRoyal Avenue Branches to live within 
their allocations from this source, the 
amount actually required was $104,631.99, 
or a saving of $5,368.01 on the budget 


R. C. HotpeNn A. D. ANDERSON 


Chairman figures. The consolidated financial statement Honorary Treasurer 


Finance Comm. Of the Metropolitan Board and Branches 


shows total operating income of $377,819.54 and expenditures of 
$377,723.46, leaving a small surplus of $96.08. 


Our Legacy Fund was increased during the year by two helpful 
bequests as follows:

Large disbursements have been made from the 
Campaign Fund on account of refurnishing of the Central, 
North, Westmount, Mount Royal Avenue, International, 
Verdun and St. Paul Branches; for the purchase of 
127,000 sq. ft. of property in Notre Dame de Grace on 
Royal and Hampton Avenues between Terrebonne and 
Monkland Avenues; and other expenditures on account 
of the new Verdun building, the contract for which has 
just been awarded. It is important to note that much 
heavier disbursements will be required in connection with

Comptroller Our Expansion Campaign programme in the near future.

Two or three rather fundamental questions have 
emerged during the year with regard to our membership 
policy and practice. The first concerns itself with the 
question of a basic membership fee. For years there has 
been dissatisfaction with the more or less casual way in 
which members have been enrolled in the Association. The Verdun 
Branch is making a special study at the present time which may result 
in making a sharp distinction between the use of privileges in their new 
building and the fact of membership. It is quite possible that they 
will recommend that a fee be charged for membership in the 
Association of say $5.00 per year in addition to which members 
will pay a specified amount for the privilege of using the equipment, such 
as gymnasium, swimming pool, tennis courts, etc. Another question 
which has come to the front during the year in this matter of membership 
is the desirability of experimenting with a family membership plan. It 
may be that in a community like Verdun, where the Association has a 
peculiar opportunity to minister to the needs of the family, the experiment 
now being carried on in other cities of issuing a membership ticket entitling 
all members of the family to use the privileges of the Association at a fee 
of say $25.00 a year, will be inaugurated. 


Basic and Family 
Membership 


Foreign Service: 


The financial support accorded the service of the 


The Y.M.C.A.— Association in sending and maintaining Canadian and 
A World-Wide American Secretaries in thirty-one countries of the world 
Movement where the “Y” is helping men and boys to establish 


indigenous Y.M.C.A’s was on a less generous basis than 
last year by $1,519.68, the amount being $20,627.60. A number of the 
Branches increased their contributions but the Special Gifts, due in part 
to the influence of our Building and Expansion Campaign, showed a 
falling off of $2,627.01.

During the period under review, 
Montreal audiences heard addresses 
on our World Service, by Mr. Harry 
W. White, on South America; John 
H. Geldart, on China; Mr. Harold G. 
Beall, on India, and M. R. Biswas of 
Calcutta, who has been a Fellowship 
Secretary on our staff since last Sep- 
tember. The most dramatic meeting, 


rs Joun H. Getpart 
Dr. Davin Z.T. Yur however, was held at the Windsor Hotel ‘Secretary 


See oa, in February when Dr. David Z. T. Yui, "91, Seraice Division 


; National Council 
General Secretary of the National 


Council of the Y.M.C.A. of China, delivered a remarkable address on the 
opportunity facing the Association in helping to build the New China, to a 
group of three hundred persons. Dr. Yui’s address was one full of hope 
for his country which has suffered severely by civil strife. In referring to 
the new Nationalist Government which has now been recognized by the 
Great Powers, he stated that of ten members in the Cabinet, seven were 
Christians and two of these are former Secretaries of the Y.M.C.A. Dr. 
Yui said that ten years ago there were one hundred Secretaries from 
Canada and the United States in China and three hundred Chinese Secre- 
taries. Two-thirds of the men from North America have been withdrawn 
and one-half of the Chinese staff enlisted by the Government. He made 
an urgent appeal for twenty more Secretaries from this Continent.

World’s Committee national Committee. Retiring Secretary 


of the Far East 


On January Ist, the Association regretfully accepted the resignation 
of one of the most beloved leaders in our Foreign Service when Mr. Fletcher 
S. Brockman, Administrative Secretary of the Far Eastern area, retired 
under the provisions of the Retirement Fund. In large measure, his 
vision and policies are responsible for the complete nationalization of our 
movement in China, and, hence, for the fortunate position in which we 
find it in that area, notwithstanding the vast changes which have taken 
place in the life and thought of the Chinese people. 


It is of the deepest interest to all that the President 

New appointment of our own Association, Mr. Gerald W. Birks, who has 
of Gerald W. Birks been a lifelong friend and generous supporter of our 
Foreign Service, entirely at his own expense is to be the 

new liaison officer acting as ambassador of good-will 

between our North American movement and the National movements in 


15 


Japan, Korea, China and the Phillippines. Colonel Birks brings to this 
great opportunity his business experience, his administrative gifts, his long 
and intimate association with our Foreign Service in = : 

the course of which he made two trips around the 
world, and an understanding of the changing 
elements in education, religion, and the Young Men’s 
Christian Association. Since his return from over- 
seas service, he has served as President of the 
Montreal Association, Chairman of the Canadian 
Foreign Service Committee, General Chairman of 
our Expansion Campaign, Chairman of our Building 
Committee; and in and through all this service has 
set an unprecedented standard in gifts of time and 
money and self. As he is to spend a part of each

National Work in Canada: 


This report would be incomplete without reference being made to the 
progress of our movement throughout the Dominion. 

The Montreal Association again shared 
in the work of our National Council and 
raised $10,500.00 toward their budget of 
$63,632.25. Its most notable contribution 
perhaps was the transfer of two of its ablest 
Senior Officers to the National staff in the 
persons of Mr. H. J. Swetman, who has 
taken over the management of the Summer 
School property at Lake Couchiching, Ont., 
José A-Macuano and Mr. R. E. G. Davis, M.A., who in pautnrse 

Chairman September became the executive head of  (2nere! Secretary. 
Can. Nat. Council’ the Personnel Division. 


The vital importance of the National Council’s service to local Asso- 
ciations in recruiting, training, placing and retiring Secretaries, has been 
recognized for many years, and the loss of these two valuable officers 
is compensated by the knowledge that they are making a contribution 
of the greatest magnitude to the solution of one of our fundamental 
problems. 


At the Annual Meeting of the Council held in London in February 
an interesting statistical statement showing the growth of the Canadian

While there is a steady increase in our work in the Dominion, it is 
not going forward nearly so rapidly as our organization in the United 
States nor as fast as the needs of our Canadian situation demands. 


Canada, politically and economically, has attained a new status 
in world affairs. A small isolated group of scattered communities in 1867, 
she now ranks fifth in commerce among the nations of the world, while 
in trade per capita she occupies the second place. In wealth per capita, 
she ranks third, following the United States and Great Britain. 


There are, however, indications that we are now in a period of de- 
velopment, new Association buildings being under construction in St. 
Catharines and our own city, while a unique contribution to Association 
architecture has been made in Midland, Ont., a town of about 10,000 
people, where a new building has recently been opened and dedicated. 
The cost was $75,000.00. This is the first modern building in Canada to 
be erected at anything like this figure. It may be that the development 
of the Association into the following cities, which have a population of 
10,000 or more, where no ““Y”’ exists at present may well be modelled on 
the Midland type of building:

The Chicago Association is studying now a suggestion that they erect 
up to twenty buildings of this type to serve primarily boys and girls, the 
effective radius being one-half mile from the building. It is proposed 
there to have one permanent Secretary on the staff and to use part-time 
men and volunteers to give volume to the work. If they embark on this 
programme it will be definitely understood that their service will include 
Hebrews and Roman Catholics without the slightest descrimination being 
made. Already in nearly all their Branches they have both these groups 
represented on their Boards of Management.

Canada would be complete without reference to the 
remarkable work being conducted by the Transportation 
Department on our two transcontinental railways directed 
by an Executive Committee composed of officials of the 
Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways with 
Mr. George Hodge, Chairman, and Mr. R. C. Vaughan, 
Vice-Chairman.

ernie ships arrived in 1928, an increase of 90 over 1927. Nine

Staff Training and Personnel: 


An organization such as ours which is 
teaching ideals to the youths of our city, 
looking towards the development of 
character and personality and a finer kind 
of society, must seek continuously to raise 
the level of its professional leadership 
with a view to making the work of the 
Association in a changing world more and 
Dr. E.M.Besr more resultful. During the year, we had x. 2. G. Davis, M.A. 

Chairman on our secretarial staff thirty full-time Secretary 


Nat. Personnel Comm. e Nat. Personnel Comm. 
and fourteen part-time men. 


Our record of staff training included the following: 

—Six of the staff attended Association Summer School at Lake 
Couchiching and Silver Bay. 

—Seven Secretaries attended the Conference of City General Secre- 
taries at Pocono where the major topic under consideration was, ‘“‘Modern 
demands on Y.M.C.A’s in Cities.” 

—Three Secretaries made studies in other cities of modern trends in 
Association buildings and programme. 

—Seven of the staff attended a Conference of Canadian General 
Secretaries where the major subject under consideration was, “Adult 
Education.” 

—Five Boys’ Work Secretaries attended the Institute held in Toronto 
to study, in company with Boys’ Work Secretaries of Ontario, various 
phases of Programme Work under the leadership of Dr. Hedley Dimock. 

—Three members of the staff took academic work at McGill University 
in the departments of Economics, English, Psychology and Philosophy, 
and one is taking an Extension Course. 

—Dr. F. O. Stredder, Mr. H. F. Hall and Mr. S. Chard were all 
members of the Faculty of the Summer School at Lake Couchiching, 
and, prior to assuming his duties with the National Council, Mr. R. E. 
G. Davis conducted the Forums at the Elgin House 
Conference of the Student Christian Movement of Canada. 


The Association has again co-operated with the 
Canadian National Council in the course for young men 
preparing for the Y.M.C.A. Secretaryship at McGill 
University by providing practical training and part-time 
employment for nine students. Mr. D. J. F. Scott, B.A., 
D. A. Bunce Mr. K. E. Norris, B.A., and Mr. C. J. McGerrigle, B.A.,

18 


Twenty of our Secretarial staff are members of the 
f Y.M.C.A. Retirement Fund. There are now 1,178 
Retirement Fund Associations and 3,502 Secretaries participating in this 
Jor Staff Officers Fund. The capital invested has a book value of $9,327,- 
645.28, the average yield on this being 5.03%. Of this 
amount the total personal accumulations of the different participating 
Secretaries is $2,580,337.29. Beginning January Ist, 1928, the employed 
officers of Scotland were admitted to the Fund. To date about twenty- 
five Scottish Secretaries have availed themselves of the privileges. Be- 
ginning July 1st, the Association Secretaries in England have been enrolled 
as their applications were received. The monthly retirement pay roll 
is now $19,927.35. There are 220 retired Secretaries to whom is sent on 
the last day of each month a cheque for the amount of their retirement 
allowance. The establishment of the Fund has been a great blessing and 
a stabilizing influence in connection with the Secretariat. 


Important changes in staff have taken place, some 
‘ of them being transfers within the movement, others 
Staff severing their connection with the Association. Recogni- 
Changes tion of the faithful and efficient services of those leaving 

us have been given during the year. 
Mr. R. E. G. Davis, M.A., tendered his resignation after eight years 
service, to take effect early in November, in order to become executive 
a o hei Personnel Division of the Canadian National Council of the 


Mr. H. J. Swetman accepted an appointment with the National 
Council of the Y.M.C.A., effective April 30th. His duties will include 
the management of the Lake Couchiching Summer School property. 


Mr. Frank B. Wilson resigned his position as Executive Secretary 
of the Mount Royal Avenue Branch, after eight years service, in order 
to enter business life, and was succeeded by Mr. Kenneth H. Murray, a 
eraduate of Springfield Y.M.C.A. College. 


Mr. A. W. Young tendered his resignation as Principal of the Sir 
George Williams College on June 30th after 29 years of service, and Dr. 
F. O. Stredder, M.A., was appointed as his successor. Mr. Young is 
continuing on the staff of the Y.M.C.A. as Principal Emeritus and Director 
of Business Courses. 


Mr. John G. MacKinnon, Executive Secretary of the North Branch, 
tendered his resignation on March 31st after fourteen years of service in 
the Central, Cote St. Paul and North Branches. 


Mr. J. M. Graham was transferred from the Employment Department 
of the Central Branch to the Executive Secretaryship of the North Branch, 
effective April Ist. 


On September Ist, Mr. Harold C. Cross took over the duties of 
Executive Secretary at the Central Branch after sixteen years of experience 
in the North Branch, Montreal; Charlottetown; overseas services during 
the war; Victoria, B.C.; and Westmount Branch, 


19 


Mr. W. J. Holliday, after a long illness, returned to duty and assumed 
the work of Secretary in charge of Counselling Service in the Central 
Branch. 


Mr. Harold E. Smith of the West End Branch, Toronto, was appointed 
Dormitory Secretary of the Central Branch on April Ist 


Mr. Geo. 8. Mooney was appointed Executive Secretary of the Verdun 
Branch where for three years he was Secretary of the Association, after 
four years experience as Young Men’s Division Secretary in Central. 


Mr. Harold G. Beall, a former member of the Dominon Square 
staff, who returned from India after spending thirteen years in that country, 
was appointed Executive Secretary of the Westmount Branch, effective 
September 15th. While in India, Mr. Beall organized the Hyderabad 
Athletic Association and the Secunderabad Interschools Sports Associa- 
tion, and introduced modern physical education into the State Schools. 
He later became Director of Branches of the Calcutta Y.M.C.A. Besides 
conducting Physical Training classes, games and sports for boys, students 
and working men in nearly all these Branches, he helped to organize the 
Bengal Olympic Association and at the request of the Government, the 
Corporation, Calcutta University and other institutions, he prepared 
schemes for physical education. 


Kamp Kanawana: 


We are pleased to report the largest 
aggregate attendance in our history. There was 
397 different boys in camp, compared with 329 
in 1927, and a total of 1,329 boy weeks, compared 
with 977 in 1927. This is an increase of 36%. 
During the “peak” week there were 268 boys 
and leaders in camp. At that time we were 
forced to refuse further applications from camp- 
ers due to lack of accommodation. 


Life in the open 


The boys came from Montreal, Westmount, Montreal West, Outre- 
mont, Maisonneuve, Pointe Claire, Verdun, Cote St. Paul, Chateauguay 
Basin, Quebec City, Thetford Mines, Ormstown, Granby, Three Rivers, 
St. Hilaire, Milltown, N.B., Toronto, Napanee, Washington, D.C., 
Havana, Cuba. 


The outstanding programme development of the 

Camp Craft and Past season was the special emphasis placed upon camp 

Handicraft Craft and handicraft. A special teacher was appointed 

: to this department. The building of a log cabin was 

undertaken, and many boys received training in the 

handling of an axe, tree-felling, building, etc. A complete set of carpentry 

tools was bought, and great interest developed in the building of bird- 
houses, canoe paddles, boats, aeroplanes, rustic furniture, etc. 


Many of the improvements about camp were the result of the labor 
of the boys themselves. The boys suggested many of these improve- 
ments, did the planning and carried out the work. In this way greater 
interest was shown, with consequent increased educational values. 


20 


Instruction was givenin a great variety 
of subjects, such as rowing, canoeing, 
bandaging, athletics, basketry, trees, boxing, 
swimming, diving, birds, archery, and life 
saving. Representative of the Forestry 
Department of Ottawa again visited camp 
and gave valuable assistance. 


R. H. Dawson Canoe trips and walking hikes were 


Chairman 


GroRGE 
conducted under careful supervision, the Porteous, B.A. 


: : Camp Direct 
aim being to help the boys learn how to 0777)" 


arrange proper shelter over night, cook for themselves, and otherwise 
develop resourcefulness in the woods and on the trail. 

Athletic and aquatic meets, swimming galas, leagues in basketball 
and volley ball, tournaments in ping-pong and tennis, circus, cuckoo 
day, camp fires, council ring, etc., etc., were as usual popular features. 


Weather conditions made it impossible to hold Sunday morning 
services in the outdoor chapel more than half the time, but all the services 
were conducted with due reverence. The morning chapel services follow- 
ing flag raising on the campus helped to weave into camp life the Christian 
principles for which our Association stands. Here an attempt was made 
to inspire motives for unselfishness, mutual helpfulness, patience and those 
other qualities which make living together happy and worth-while. The 
evening devotions in each tent, led by the tent-leader had a profound 
effect on the lives of the boys. Inspirational talks, Sunday song services 
around the fire and on the lake, all helped toward the achievement of the 
right camp spirit. 


Sunday collections amounting to $63.60 were as usual donated to 
our Foreign Service. 

The new Lodge was finally completed, 
with hardwood floors, sheathing, and an 
attractive big fireplace. We are greatly in- 
debted to Mrs. R. M. Cushing for a complete 
set of beautiful curtains for the windows ard 
doors. Mrs. Cushing previously donated the 
furniture for the building and has always been 
a kind friend of the camp. 

The Council Ring was rebuilt and enlarged 
to accommodate 325 people. It is now 
regarded as one of the finest in Canada. 


A Class in Baskelry 


Two new rowboats, a sailing canoe, seven new tents, ten new tent 
floors, two dozen blankets, and four new hospital beds were added. A 
fine square piano, chapel organ and a new portable Orthophonic, the 
donation of Mr. E. M. Berliner, were secured. A new canoe wharf and 
Junior Camp was a badly needed improvement. 


The Fossils Club of Westmount Branch again provided camp scholar- 
ships for thirteen underprivileged boys, chosen through the Branches. 
Another group of Westmount business men and dormitory residents paid 
the expenses of fifteen boys from the Orphan’s Home and two boys from 
the School for the Blind. 


21 


The season was a record one financially. Camp receipts totalled 
$13,765.63 as compared with $11,460.00 last year, an increase of $2,305.63. 
The operating expenses were $12,872.22, leaving a surplus of $893.41 to 
apply on the cost of the new lodge erected two years ago. This is especially 
gratifying when we remember thatZour weekly fee is only $8.50, our aim 
being to keep the cost within reach of the average home in our city. 


The greatly increased attendance at Kanawana in 

Enlargement of | 1928, combined with a growing recognition of the remark- 

Kamp Kanawana ®ble Christian education opportunities which inhere in 

camping, has resulted in the decision to enlarge the enter- 

prise by building a new camp site on the shores of Lac 

Beescies, which is within twenty minutes’ walk of the administrative 

centre of Kanawana. It is expected that this will take care of a large 

number of boys who desire to attend camp and at the same time not 
imperil the effectiveness of our camp service by overcrowding. 


Camp Otoreke: 

The attendance of young men at Camp 
Otoreke totalled 211 as against 160 the previous 
year. This is within five of the record attendance 
in the year 1920. A great deal of attention was 
given to improving the camp equipment, the 
result being altogether favorable. The finan- 
cial statement for the year showed $4,492.44 
receipts and $4,407.83 expenditures. The 
Metropolitan Board has loaned $2,000.00 to the 

ae cde Camp Committee for the purpose of increasing 

the accommodation and modernizing the 

Pe a some of which has been in use since the camp was organized 
in : 


Camp Dorval: 

Camp Dorval was again operated jointly by the Verdun and Cote 
St. Paul Branches using the large house leased from the Marcil Trust 
Company in 1925. Eighty-one boys spent 214 week-ends in this camp, 
which was operated for two full weeks and ten week-ends. We have 
experimented with the idea of a ‘“Near-the-city’”’ camp for older boys and 
have found that there is a very important need for such an enterprise. 
The facilities available, however, are so inadequate that unless some 
property can be secured which will better meet the needs of the situation, 
it is proposed to discontinue this service. 


Metropolitan Boys’ Work: 

Probably the outstanding event of the year was 
the splendid part taken by the Boys’ Division in the 
Expansion Campaign last Spring. The teams were led 
by boys, and their campaign, was conducted by the same 
methods as the Men’s Division. Their enthusiasm meant 
a aia great deal to the success of the Campaign as a 
whole. 


At the close of the last school year, the graduating 


° . 2% Netson McEwen 
classes of the various High Schools of Montreal and Secretary 


district, were invited by the S.C.A. of McGill and the M4yvopelilan Boys: 


22 


Y.M.C.A. to attend a special supper meeting, when the prospective 
students of the University were given helpful information regarding ways 
in which they might make the most of college life, especially by establishing 
right contacts in their freshman year. The nucleus of this group of 
older boys was made up of members of our various Hi-Y Clubs in the city. 


It was recognized this year that there would be distinct 
advantage in holding all the Annual Father and Son 
Banquets on one evening. On November 24th, therefore, 
six Branches were hosts to the boys and dads, and 1,444 
attended the banquets. This represented a considerable 
increase in attendance over anything in previous years. Outstanding 
speakers, toasts, music, etc., helped to develop the right spirit of comrad- 
ship and understanding between fathers and sons. ‘This we believe to be 
one of the most significant things in our Boys’ Work programme. 


Father and Son 
Banquets 


In October, we were favored with a visit from Mr. Henri Johannot 
of the Boys’ Work staff of the World’s Committee, with headquarters at 
Geneva, Switzerland. A special luncheon was tendered him at the Mount 
Royal Hotel, and a rally of the employed boys’ members of all Branches 
took place at Central, when Mr. Johannot told of the progress of our 
Association Boys’ Work in Europe. 


The Inter-Branch programme event involving the 


City-wide largest educational values was undoubtedly the annual 
Boys’ Hobby — Boys’ Hobby Show. Representative boys from the 
Show Branches form the Board of Directors, and during several 


months of continuous work they plan and carry out all 
the details of the show. This included the building up of the programme, 
securing of section directors, printing of prize lists, securing of advertising 
and prizes, publicity, enlisting judges, preparing display of exhibits, etc. 
Not only does the show provide a splendid training for the boys who are 
responsible, but each year in an increasing way it is encouraging the boys 
of the city to take an interest in worth-while hobbies. It is open to all 
boys. 


During the year the Association participated with other Boys’ Work 
organizations of the city in plans to establish a Boy Life Council, and took 
an active part in the work known as “Boys’ Week”’. 


The promotion of Kamp Kanawana was in the hands of this Com- 
mittee, co-operating with the Kanawana Committee, and included the 
very successful camp re-union, which brought together two hundred of 
last year’s campers at Westmount Branch. 


The annual basketball and ping-pong tournaments and swimming 
championships were conducted with splendid competition, and close 
interest, all Branches taking part. Model aircraft work has also been 
one of the big Association activities for boys. 


Religious Work: 


In the reports of the various Branches to their Annual Meetings, 
reference has been made to the many methods used to interpret the 
spiritual objectives of the Association to the young men and boys in its

membership. These have taken the form of personal interviews, discus- 
sion and study groups, conferences and forums, fireside sing songs, Sunday 
afternoon musicales, campfire talks and devotions, vesper services, resident 
members’ breakfasts, foreign service meetings, observance of the Week 
of Prayer, and many other events. 


In a rapidly changing civilization in which material 
Youth inarapidly advances threaten to outrun our social, moral and spiritual 
changing ability to grapple with new problems as they are intro- 
civilization duced, the Y.M.C.A. attempts experimentally to find a 
substitute for the authoritatianism of the past generation 
which youth no longer accepts. There is great uncertainty in such areas 
as sex and family life, religion and morals, international relationships, 
the ethics of business and forms of government. Thoughtful people 
agree that some ultimate principle must be found or civilization itself 
will be menaced. The new situation would seem to demand that we 
recognize that our old educational system is inadequate; that the modern 
industrial world makes new educational demands; that scientific teaching 
replace the blind acceptance of tradition; that critical mindedness become 
a characteristic attitude of our day, and that youth discover for itself the 
mind of Jesus for their day and generation. 


One of the most serious attempts in the life of con- 
temporaneous movements to grapple with the pressing 
problems of our day has been made through the medium 
of the Young Men’s Forum in our Central Branch which 
this season held seventeen meetings, discussing the 
general theme, “Looking toward a more Christian Social Order.” The 
programme was undertaken after conference with ministers and business 
men as a means of stimulating thought and discussion upon a number of 
questions relating to the existing industrial order which are troubling the 
minds and consciences of many to-day. It was planned to consider the 
consequences that would result from the frank application of the ethical 
teachings of Jesus to these questions, and the method followed was that 
of an impartial enquiry. 


Young Men’s 
Forum 


Prof. Harry F. Ward summarized the principles of Jesus for society 
as follows: 
—Gnun is the Father of all men, 
—AU men are therefore brothers. 
—fvuery human personality is sacred, and, 
—the strong must help the weak.

Metropolitan Physical Education: 


Physical education during the past year has main- 
tained its place in the Montreal Association as the most 
attractive feature of our activities. 


Gymnasium classes have been conducted by all of 
the eight Branches, with five full time Physical Directors 
and the others with part-time or voluntary leadership, 
or directed by the Secretaries. The Senior Leaders’ Corps 
at Central, Westmount and North Branches rendered 

J.K.MecNurr Valuable assistance, and Junior Corps in these and other 

Chairman Branches were developed to help in the Boys’ Work. 

The annual Leaders’ Corps conference of Quebec Province 

and Ottawa Valley was held on December Ist and 2nd in the Westmount 
Branch with 45 delegates present. 


Medical examinations were given prominence at Central. 

Boxing, wrestling and fencing were promoted, the latter by the 
North Branch. who developed a good team with several meets, and Central 
had probably the best and largest classes in the city in the two former. 
Representatives of the Canadian boxing and wrestling team at the Am- 
sterdam Olympic Meet were from Central, and Central’s wrestling in- 
structor was coach to the Canadian team. Four Provincial boxing cham- 
pionships were won by Central Branch this Spring, and our men gave 
splendid examples of good sportmanship in open competition. 


Basketball has maintained its popularity, all Branches playing, with 
hundreds of men and boys, in house leagues throughout the winter. The 
Inter-Branch Boys’ Championships were well contested. Westmount 
won the City League Intermediate Championship and also the Provincial. 


Handball and badminton increased in popularity at Central, North 
and Westmount, as also did volley ball at the two former. Bowling, 
however, has lost its drawing power except at Point St. Charles. West- 
mount and North Branches have done away with their alleys and now use 
the space for Boys’ Work and handball respectively, while Central has 
only three of its six alleys in use. 


28 


Hockey was popular at several Branches during the winter. 

Swimming classes were promoted during the summer, and hundreds 
of children taught to swim; while Canadian proficiency badges were won 
by swimmers in the Boys’ Divisions. The annual Boys’ Inter-Branch 
Swimming Meet was successfully conducted and was won by Central. 


Ladies’ and girls’ physical work was carried on by Mount Royal 
Avenue and Westmount Branches, Mount Royal renting their quarters 
to the Y.M.C.A. one day per week, and Westmount having regular weekly 
gymnasium classes and swimming periods in the mornings and early after- 
noons. Ladies’ badminton was very popular at Westmount. 


In athletics, Central and North Branches had teams in city meets. 
North Branch again conducted the Dunlop Trophy Road Race last Fall, 
and won for the second year in succession. 


Tennis courts to the number of twenty were maintained by Point 
St. Charles, St. Paul, North and Westmount Branches, which were patron- 
ized to the full. 


City-Wide Relationships: 


The Y.M.C.A. in its effort to enrich the life of the 

Aclive co-operation City in which our primary work among young men is 

with many carried forward has recognized its relationship to other 

organizations organizations working in the field of religion, social service 

and education. It has sought to conscientiously ally 

itself to many of these agencies, and has been able to accomplish much in 
co-operation which would have been quite impossible otherwise.

Sir George Williams College: 


Ten hundred and twenty different men and women, 
boys and girls, have been students in the College during 


pp lid the year. This represents an increased enrolment over 

: last year of 95. The students were registered in the 
various divisions as follows:

Of the 1,020 students 368 were sixteen years of age or under. The 
median age was 17.93 years. 


; It will be recognized that the registration and assimi- 

Boop oe lation of over one thousand students has involved a great 

ee, ! deal of counselling and guidance with regard to suitable 

Guidance courses. A great part of the time of the Executive Staff 

has been given under the direction of Mr. H. F. Hall. 

Student Counsellor, to this work. Students properly placed at the 

beginning of the term usually continue successfully to the end of the 
season. 


Faculty 
Sir George Williams College 


A new feature of the guidance programme which has been inaugurated 
this session is that of an Orientation Course for all new students in the 
High School Course. Mr. Hall has three such classes, with about sixty 
students in each class, meeting one hour a week each for the whole session. 
The aims of the Orientation Course are: First, to teach students how to 


3] 


study effectively, by developing efficient study habits; a special text-book 
is used in connection with this part of the course. Second, to give the 
students a background of information regarding occupations in Canada 
and to teach them how to analyse and to evaluate occupations from the 
point of view of their own life-work choices. Third, to enable these 
students to gain a knowledge of the rules and practices of healthful living. 


We feel that the establishment of this Orientation Course is another 
step in the direction of character education. 


The members of the executive staff unfortunately do not have a 
great deal of time at their disposal for participation in outside educational 
activities. Four such activities, however, should be mentioned. 


1. Mr. H. F. Hall delivered a series of four lectures, during the fall 
months, on “The Curriculum of Religious Education’, under the 
auspices of the Diocesan Board of Religious Education, in connec- 
tion with a training class for Sunday School teachers. The course 
was most successful, over one hundred being present at each of 
the sessions. 

2. The Principal has had the privilege of serving, during the past 
year and a half, on the “Vocational Guidance Committee of 
Montreal.” The chief result of this committee’s work has been 
the production of a report of a survey of vocational schools and 
opportunities in Montreal. 

3. The Student Counsellor, Mr. H. F. Hall, acted as a professional 
advisor to the Negro Community Centre in connection with a 
‘Find Yourself Campaign’ which they held during February. 
He also gave an address on the subject of ‘“The Choice of a Voca- 
tion,’”’ at one of the meetings of the campaign. 

4. The Principal and the Student Counsellor collaborated on a 
course on the “Psychological Aspects of Personal Guidance” 
which was given at the Y.M.C.A. Summer School at Lake Cou- 
chiching. 


The year has been most encouraging. The registra- 
Insufficient. _ tion has been a record one although, unfortunately, many 
accommodalion students have had to be refused admission during the 
for students year as they could not be accommodated. There is 
definite evidence of the development of a fine esprit de 
corps, a difficult thing to achieve among part-time students. The admin- 
istrative and instructional staff has been able to make progress in the 
working out of some difficult problems of curriculum and method. Definite 
improvement has been made in our counselling programme and the devel- 
opment of orientation courses in the High School. Provision has been 
made for the addition of a full-time Registrar and Bursar to the staff. 


This progress results, of course, from the fact that the Association has 
been able to meet, in a very practical way, the need for supplementary edu- 
cational facilities in Montreal. As such formal educational programmes 
as the Association offers have inherent in them the highest possibilities 
for the enrichment of personality and development of character, it is 
proper that every effort should be made to provide adequate facilities 
for this work and that the largest possible number of young people should 
be enlisted in these programmes. 


32 


Central Branch: 


An adequate description of the work carried out in 
Central Branch during the year would take more space 
than can be spared in this Report. A few items of interest 
may be referred to briefly. 


As usual, a great deal of the time of Central staff, 
and building space, has been devoted to the service of 
non-members. Particularly has this been true during 
the past year with reference to the very large number of 
young men immigrating to Canada from the British Isles 

The proposed Nw and Europe. Many of these came with letters of 
Teg madnt introduction from Y.M.C.A. Secretaries at their ports 

of embarkation, or home cities, and we attempt so to 
assist them that they will realize the world-wide aspect of our Association 
brotherhood. 


During the past year 3,847 young men 
were housed in Central Building; 3,243 
were classed as transients; 604 registered 
for two weeks or longer. Many national- 
ities, many creeds and many occupations 
were represented in our rather large family. 
Many young men have been turned away 
because accommodation was not available. 
This was especially true in the summer 


Lr.-Con. Herserr x Harnotp C, Cross 
NELL months. Executive Secretary 
Chairman 


The residents elected their own council, 
and this group has carried out a very effective programme in the interests 
of the dormitory men. This included the Sunday morning breakfast, 
Hike Club, social evenings, issuance of the ‘“‘Dormat.’’ The council also 
undertook to welcome newcomers to the building. 


The Young Men’s Division has enjoyed an active 
year. Worthwhile activities have included the Young 
Men’s Conference at Isle aux Cerfs, at which the Asso- 
ciation programme, as it affects young men, was carefully 
considered; two Y.M.-Y.W. study groups, composed. of 
young men and young women, who have studied the life 
and teachings of Jesus; the Y’s Men’s Club, which has 
conducted a very successful season; the Dramatic Club; 
H.J.Hannavonn the Bible Study group studying “Jesus in the Records;” 

Wee-Chairman several other clubs and discussion groups; the Sunday 
afternoon musicales; socials; tournaments, etc. 


Few people realize what a really fine library is available at Central. 
An attempt is made to keep adding a selection of the new books as they 
come out, and a splendid assortment of Canadian, British and American 
magazines is kept on file. The total circulation of books for the year was 
17,376, an increase of 2,000 over last year. 


33 


The Boys’ Division membership reached the high total of 798 this 
past year. A striking fact is that 80% of these boys are employed either 
full time or after school, indicating the type of boy reached. The Boys’ 
Cabinet, elected by the boys, has done a splendid piece of work in leader- 
ship of the various activities. An encouraging feature of the year’s 
programme was the increased interest on the part of the parents of the 
boys. This was evidenced in the Father and Son Banquets, at both of 
which the large hall was filled to capacity. 


The Hobby Show, Hospital Choir, Moving Pictures, Discussion 
Groups and Conferences have provided opportunities for growth and 
development. 


The aggregate attendance at all features of the Physical Department 
for the year was 98,285, an increase over last year of over 10,000. Eight 
free swimming campaigns were held and 336 physical examinations were 
given to men and boys. 


Central is justly proud of the fact that three repre- 
sentatives of its boxing and wrestling clubs were sent to 
the Olympic games at Amsterdam, and also supplied the 
wrestling coach, Mr. Frank Saxon. The Senior, Inter- 
mediate and Junior Leaders’ Corps carried on a weekly 
course of training and service, accepting responsibility 
for the leadership of the evening gymnasium classes. A 
marked increase in the interest and attendance at hand- 


° atte Sypney CHarp 
ball was shown during the year. Thirty teams played Director of Physical 


: Educal 
in two-house basketball leagues. The Branch was also Seed 


represented in the city basketball league. 


During the past year, greater emphasis than ever 
before has been placed on the counselling and guidance of 
members. This has been possible through the appoint- 
ment of a Secretary to give time full to this work. Greater 
care has been taken, when a man joined, to try to find 
out his interests and needs. An attempt has been made 
to follow up new members to discover the degree of satisfac- 
tion they have experienced in their connection with the 

W. J. Houupay Association. To many, a wider participation in the 

“Secretary programme has been suggested. As a result, there has 

been a better assimilation of these new members. Then, 

too, the Association is being increasingly appreciated as a “fellowship” 
rather than an institution chiéfly engaged in selling privileges. 


This Counselling Service extends to all other members who desire 
it, and has to do with vocational adjustments, further educational prepara- 
tion, establishment of desirable social contacts, health problems, employ- 
ment, religious questions, home relationships, and other personal matters, 


34 


An important service was rendered through the 
Employment Department during the year. Thirteen 
hundred and twenty-seven different persons were inter- 
viewed, and of these 741 definitely registered for employ- 
ment. Three hundred and fifteen men and boys were 
placed in positions, mostly permanent. Scores of well- 
known firms have been assisted through this means. 


The splendid work of the Ladies’ Auxiliary, which 

has just completed its twenty-ninth season, should be 

Ps nee b pa mentioned. They have given very helpful assistance at 

banquets and social events, and have sent flowers to Associ- 

ation members who were ill. Their service has been greatly appreciated. 

The total expenditures for the year were $167,210.14, the income 

including $16,735.00 from the Joint Fund being $165,788.98, leaving an 
operating deficit of $1,421.16. 


Westmount Branch: 


A most successful year was closed with a 
membership of 852, of whom 481 were boys, 
which is a record membership in this Divis- 
ion. It is interesting to note that 602 
different boys were members during the 
year, of whom 88% were school boys and 
12% business boys. Fifty-six per cent are 
living in Westmount, thirty-nine per cent 
in Notre-Dame de Grace, three per cent in 
J.B. Frosstr ~~ Montreal West, and two per cent elsewhere. Hanoxp G._ 

C < ‘ Beat, B.P.E. 
Protestants numbered 86%, Roman Catho-  grecutire Secretary 
ics 7%, Hebrews 5%, and others 2%. 


There are 18 organized clubs, with the usual discussion groups, socials 
and competitions, and special events such as the Father and Son Dinner, 
when 427 fathers and sons were present. The Hi-Y Club has a membership 
of 43. The model airplane club with 81 members is the largest in Montreal, 
and is officially styled the “Pioneer Chapter” of the Junior Aviation League 
of Canada, Montreal Branch, it being the first organized on the Montreal 
Island. It has participated in 11 flying meets, winning the majority of 
the awards and holding two duration records. 


The Men’s Division has had an active year, participating in the observ- 
ance of the World-Wide Week of Prayer. The Fossils Club has had 
another excellent year. Their annual show netted over $400.00, which 
will be used again to send fifteen boys to Camp on a scholarship arrange- 
ment. The Dormitory Council and Spoke Club were two new organiza- 
tions during the year. The Physical Department enrolled in their gymna- 
sium classes 562, an increase of 29% over last year and 65% of the entire 
membership. Handball has grown in popularity to such an extent that 
a third court has been added to the gymnasium. Badminton has an 
enrollment of 76, of whom 56 are women, and a waiting list of 25. Volley 
ball and boxing were also carried on regularly while the basketball season 
was an outstanding one in history, the Intermediate team winning the 
Provincial Championship with an excellent record of sportsmanship. Two 
gymnasium exhibitions were given by the three Leaders’ Corps, which now 


35 


have a total membership of 62. The Senior Leaders’ corps won the Lemuel 
Cushing trophy in the city-wide competition. The Tennis Club enrolled 
160 members while softball leagues in Westmount Park were popular and 
12 teams played hockey on the Westmount City rinks. 


The privileges of the swimming pool have been extended to the 
Verdun and Cote St. Paul Branches weekly, and to school and church groups 
on special occasions. Nine of the Senior Leaders conducted gymnasium 
classes weekly for the boys of the School for the Blind, the Mackay 
Institute for the Deaf and Dumb, the Protestant Orphanage, and the 
St. Henri Baptist Mission. In the early summer 125 boys and girls 
under ten years of age enrolled for swimming, 112 of them being taught 
to swim. Progressive programmes of tests were given and 200 National 
professional certificates given to boys in the membership. An interesting 
programme of work is being carried on for women and girls as follows:— 
Ladies’ gymnasium classes are conducted two mornings per week, and 
swimming two mornings per week. Girls’ classes in swimming are con- 
ducted Saturday mornings, and the gymnasium is used for Badminton 
each day except Saturday. The women have equal privileges with men 
on tennis courts, while the girls of Westmount High School use the swim- 
ming pool twice a week and gymnasium classes are conducted for the 
Sunnyside School two mornings each week. 


The total receipts for the year were $37,373.26 with expenditures of 
$37,348.85, leaving a surplus of $24.51. Of this amount $5,445.00 was 
received from the Joint Fund and $1,000.00 from the Expansion Campaign 
Fund. 


The extraordinary service of the Women’s Auxiliary was a big factor 
in the success of the Year’s work. 


North Branch: 


The past twelve months have been 
marked by steady progress in membership, 
programme and esprit de corps. The great- 
est advance registered during the year was 
in the field of Boys’ Work, the membership 
having increased from 176 to 375, this being 
in addition to the boys who participated in 
various community activities on a non- 
membership basis. 


J. M. Granam 
W. J. Moore Executive Secretary 


Chairman 


The Father and Son Banquet, attended 
by over 250, was a high-water mark in 
point of attendance. The quality and quantity of informal, education 
groups or ‘interest’ clubs was mbst gratifying, there being a total of twelve 
covering the field of rifle shooting, model aircraft, basketry, public speak- 
ing, mandolin, swimming, electrical, mouth organ, dramatic, glee, Meccano 
and photography clubs. In the physical department, fencing, track and 
field athletics, national and international hexathlon contests, swimming 
meets, basketball leagues, badminton club, gymansium Leaders’ Corps, 
hockey, wrestling and boxing clubs all had a good season. The tennis 


36 


activities as carried on, on the new property in the Town of Mount Royal, 
where there were eight new courts, had a very successful year. 


The financial statement for the year showed a total operating expense 
of $26,079.65 with income of $25,478.36, leaving a deficit of $601.29. 


The resignation of John G. MacKinnon was announced and accepted 
with very great regret after his many years of useful service in the Asso- 
ciation movement. The new Executive Secretary, J. M. Graham, was 
introduced to the annual meeting as one who has had wide Association 
experience in St. Catharines, Vancouver and the Central Y.M.C.A. in 
Montreal. 


Point St. Charles and Turcot: 


The Point St. Charles Branch is a co- 
operative effort in which the Y.M.C.A. 
joins with the Canadian National Railways 
in financing the work, while the Turcot 
Branch is entirely financed by the Canadian 
National Railways. 


Fourteen teams have participated in

events was most gratifying. During the winter a fancy dress carnival was

In addition to the service in Point St. Charles, the Branch at Turcot 
has been operated throughout the year, being open twenty-four hours each 
day. <A total of 7,500 beds were used by the men on the railroad, and 
23,000 meals partaken in the building. In addition to this, a very im- 
portant service of a miscellaneous character was rendered to firemen, 
brakesmen and others who used the Branch continually. 


The financial statement showed an income of $8,220.78 and an 
expenditure of $8,203.04, leaving a surplus of $17.74 for the year. 


Verdun Branch: 


The Verdun Branch passed its tenth 
milestone on March 13th, having taken 
five important steps in its history. The 
Association was first located on Rielle 
Avenue, then moved to more commodious 
offices on Church Avenue. Four years later 
they moved to Wellington Street, where 
after two years they doubled the accommo-

During the year an important co-operative service has been carried 
on with the Night Schools, homes and churches and the municipality. 
The recreational activities were attended by 1,033 people, the most 
popular events being playground ball and hockey. The community 
singing was again carried on on the dyke, with a weekly attendance of 
approximately 4,500. The Association Secretary again acted as district 
convenor for the Q.A.H.A., and general supervisor of the activities on the 
municipal rinks. Seventy-one teams were organized in all, with a total 
of 690 players. The Chief of Police states that juvenile delinquents are 
very much fewer when the playgrounds and rinks are in operation. Organi- 
zations co-operated with during the year include the Clansmen, I.0.D.E., 
District Scoutmasters, Olivert Baptist Church, Montreal Parks and Play- 
erounds Association. 


The expenditures for the year total $5,367.91 with income of $4,877.56, 
leaving a deficit of $490.35. 


The Board of Management is keenly aware of the task of making 
a thorough study of the trends in modern Association theory and practice 
with a view to realizing the very best possible in the new building which 
it is expected will be opened during the year. 


Cote St. Paul: 


The building on Gladstone Avenue, which has been 
so generously placed at our disposal by the Protestant 
Board of School Commissioners, has been completely 
renovated during the year and has again been used by the 
community to very great advanatge. 


Educational classes included first aid classes for the 
employees of industries; and educational trips to the 
following firms had an average attendance of 41. Steel 
Company of Canada, Montreal Daily Star, Bell Telephone,

A visit to McGill University was made when Prof. Judah lectured on 
“Human Anatomy,” this lecture having an attendance of 73. 


A library of 560 volumes, presented by the Rotary and Kiwanis 
Clubs, was used by 240 boys during the year. 


Co-operation with the night school authorities in Cote St. Paul 
resulted in 61 pupils attending the classes. 


Hobbies for boys were encouraged, and moving picture shows given. 
Physical activities included 12 teams in soccer football, enrolling 142 
players; 36 members in the tennis club; 12 basketball teams enrolled 64 
players; the road race had 22 entries; 30 boys were taught to swim in the 
Westmount Y.M.C.A. pool; a boxing class was conducted with an average 
attendance of 16 per week; gymnasium classes were organized and hockey 
was carried on with 32 teams enrolling 332 players; Fourfold clubs for 
boys were organized; the Young Men’s Conference at Isle aux Cerfs,

Mount Royal Avenue: 


The resignation of Mr. Frank B. Wilson 
in June was a severe loss to the Association. 
Mr. K. H. Murray was appointed to succeed 
him in September and a useful season’s work 
was reported at the Annual Meeting. 


The gymnasium classes had a total 
attendance of 5,193; 1,920 swims were had 
at the North Branch; 1,439 showers were 

he taken; 718 participated in softball; 423 *- aa

Chairman participated in soccer; 610 participated in Executive Secretary 
hockey. A ten lesson swimming campaign 
was organized during the summer with an average attendance of 68 every 
morning. We were able to render this service through the courtesy of 
the North Branch Y.M.C.A. Our gymnasium exhibition was held on 
March 26th with an estimated attendance of 275. <A billiard table was 
secured, and the reading room was redecorated to make things more 
attractive for the young men. 


A Sunday afternoon programme for young men was attempted this 
year for the first time, and was found to be very successful. Speakers were 
provided by the Religious Work Committee on various subjects. Four 
hundred and thirty-eight were present during the season, with an average 
of 24 each Sunday. Our Young Men’s Conference on the “Church and 
the Young Man” was highly successful. We were fortunate in securing 
the services of Mr. L. A. Buckley of the Y.M.C.A. National Council as 
our leader. Fifty-two different people attended the Conference and 12 
different Churches were represented. 


Our Young Men’s Social Committee had a pleasant season. One 
hundred and fifteen young people were present at our opening social. 
We had five socials under the auspices of this Committee with an attendance 
of 389. A few Y.W.-Y.M.C.A. socials were held during the year. One 
hundred and forty-five boys were present at our Hallowe’en parties and 
had a spooky time. Opening banquets were held for the school boys with 
an attendance of 84. Eighty boys and fathers attended our Father and 
Son Banquet. The object of this banquet is to better the relationship 
between the father and son. Mr. Harold C. Cross was the speaker. The 
Ladies’ Auxiliary held a Boys’ Night for the members and their friends. 
One hundred and forty-nine boys were present.

Progress With New Buildings: 


Notwithstanding the problems facing us because of 

Verdun, the incompletion of the Expansion Campaign Fund, the 

St. Paul, Metropolitan Board has proceeded as rapidly as possible 

Pt. St. Charles with the forward movement of the Association. After 

years of waiting on the part of the citizens in the district 

south of the Canal, their dream of a modern Y.M.C.A. building is coming 

true. Following arduous work on the part of the architects, and 

eighteen meetings of the Building Committee, the contract for the 

Verdun-St. Paul-Point St. Charles building has been awarded to the 

James Shearer Company, and it is expected that ground will be broken 
during the first week of May. 


The building has been designed by 
Messrs. Nobbs & Hyde and is of Georgian 
type of architecture. The exterior is Neu-tone 
Rustic brick and Indiana limestone. It will 
have a cubic content of 410,000 feet and will 
contain social rooms with fireplaces for men, 
women and boys; gymnasium, swimming pool 
and shower rooms; auditorium and banquet 


Nei Verdun-St.Péul- hall; reading rooms; club rooms for debating 
Point St. Charles Building societies and religious discussion groups; class 


rooms for informal educational work including 
handicraft class in wood working and metal working; boys’ club rooms, 
one of the latter being designed as a ship’s cabin. The building will be 
constructed with Canadian materials wherever possible, and will be located 
at the south end of the property recently acquired on Gordon Avenue, 
which will also accommodate six tennis courts, soccer football field, four 
playground baseball diamonds, hockey and skating rinks, and will serve 
a district with a population of over 100,000 persons. 


Central Extension We are glad to report that the plans for the alterations 
and to the present Drummond Street building and the erection 

Notre Dame de of the College and Dormitory building on Stanley Street 
Grace are nearing completion; that 127,000 square feet of 


property has been purchased on Royal and Hampton 
Avenues, Notre Dame de Grace, for the erection of a building in that 
district; and that the quarters occupied by the International Branch in 
the new Bank of Commerce building on St. Catherine Street East have 
been entirely re-furnished in a manner which is most pleasing and which 
has been an important factor in the extraordinary advances made in their 
work during the past year.

Changing It is interesting at this point to reflect upon the 
Architecture of _ history of Association architecture. In the first period 
¥Y.M.C.A. the work of the ‘Y’ was carried on in social parlors and 

Buildings reading rooms usually located on an upper floor over a 

store. Later buildings revealed that the programme 
emphasis was on religious meetings. In this period there was usually 
the semblance of a church spire on one corner of the building. In the next 
period, gymnasiums and dormitories made their appearance. The build- 
ings then reflected the industrial and commercial life of our great cities, 
being very much like factory or office buildings in appearance and with 
purely utilitarian walls and partitions. As young men poured into our 
great cities following the industrial revolution of the last century, an ever 
increasing number of dormitories and dining rooms and social rooms were 
provided to meet their needs. Enlarging horizons in office and factory 
brought to the Association its vocational educational programme. 


To provide adequate facilities for all of these pro- 

Contribution of — grammes and services under one roof for distinct groups 
Architectural and ages and to permit of adequate administration and 
Bureau teaching was a problem too difficult for any one architect. 

It is not surprising, therefore, that most buildings showed 

a lack of experience in co-ordinating these many functions. To meet the 
needs of a difficult situation, there has arisen in the Association movement 
the Architectural Bureau, which, during the last ten years, has by a process 
of group-thinking by secretaries, business men, architects, engineers and 
designers produced a body of experience available for all local Associations. 
They have, by study and observation of wasted areas and unused 
equipment, reduced building and operating costs and multiplied efficiency. 
This has naturally resulted in smaller boiler and heating units, smaller 
wash rooms, fewer toilet facilities, narrower corridors and smaller rooms. 
It should be remembered that the income from a Y.M.C.A. dormitory for 
one week is about the same as it is for a hotel for one night, and that the 
annual membership fee in the Association is a very moderate one indeed. 


Within the last four years the “no basement” plan has been evolved 
for smaller buildings which must be manned by few people and this is 
the type being erected in Verdun. This has brought the swimming pool 
up to the first floor level, and has thereby reduced greatly costs of 
supervision, especially during the less busy hours of the day. 


Perhaps the most conspicuous change in the past ten 
years has been the stress upon aesthetic values. This 
has resulted from architect, artist and craftsman working 
together producing new designs in buildings and furniture 
and a harmony in the use of color which awakens admira- 
tion and respect. To secure’ attractive interiors does not necessarily 
involve greater expenditure than dull and sombre effects. Color and 
decoration in gymnasiums, swimming pools and social rooms do not need 
to add to the cost. The rising standards of excellence in many areas of 
life to-day makes it imperative that the Association in its buildings should 
combine beauty and durability while planning buildings which may be 
adapted to changing programmes.

aesthetic values

Obituary: 


We are sorry to record the removal by death of members and friends 
of the Association as follows: 


Mrs. John Archibald. R. B. Hayes. 
Walter R. Baker. J. W. Knox. 

R. M. Ballantyne. H. J. Jackson. 
Henry Birks. P. V. Lamoise. 

J. F. Bannister. J.S. Mackenzie. 
Miss Annie H. Brown. Sir Vincent Meredith. 
R. H. Buchanan. F. W. Molson. 
H. D. Cantlon. Fred. J. Shaw. 
Mrs. T. J. Dawson. Lady Van Horne. 
Sir Lomer Gouin. J. C. Watson. 

A. C, Harlow. H. W. Weller. 


Geo. A. Warburton. 


Included in this number were Mr. J. W. Knox, a past President and 
one who for over thirty years was a Director of the Association; Mr. 
R. H. Buchanan, who was a Director for forty-five years, and Mr. Henry 
Birks who for over fifty years was intimately connected with our Y.M. 
C.A. and gave with unfailing generosity to its ever enlarging needs and 
opportunities not only in this City but throughout the Dominion and the 
world. Appropriate resolutions of appreciation and sympathy have been 
recorded in the Minutes of the Metropolitan Board. 


Appreciation: 


There are many factors which combine to make possible a successful 
year’s work in the Y.M.C.A. We are grateful to the many friends who 
have contributed generously of their financial resources; to the workers 
in the Financial, Membership and other campaigns; to members of Boards 
and Comittee for their frequent counsel, guidance and service; to the 
many volunteers who have served as friendly counsellors of clubs; inter- 
viewers; speakers; teachers; interpreters; ministers; to the members of 
the Leaders’ Corps; the Staff; to the Churches; the Women’s Auxiliaries; 
the Protestant Board of School Commissioners; Railroad and other corpor- 
ations; Parks and Playground Association; the Young Women’s Christian 
Association, and many other co-operating agencies. Above all, we are in 
humility grateful to God for His blessing and power. 


Conclusion: 


As we close this record of another year’s service may we not think of 
all this work as a spiritual sanctuary which we are building to God through 
the years. Like Solomon’s temple in olden times, which was builded in 
silence, without noise of tools or machinery, so the temple of the inner life 
of this movement rises silently, taking on such proportions and features 
as our thoughts and deeds from day to day determine. In the rearing 
of this unseen temple our moral and religious motives are reinforced by a 


43 


certain artistic impulse, such as that which gives the architect of a noble 
building his chief inspiration. 


“There is an architecture grander far 

Than all the fortresses of War, 

More inextinguishably bright 

Than learning’s lonely towers of light. 
Framing its walls of faith and hope and love 
In deathless souls of men, it lifts above 

The frailty of our earthly home 

An everlasting dome; 

The sanctuary of the human host, 

The living temple of the Holy Ghost.” 


Henry Van Dyke (‘“The Builders.”’)

FORMS FOR CLAUSES IN WILLS 


The following forms for clauses in Wills may be found to be convenient by those who 
contemplate making testamentary provision for the Association 


For General Purposes 
I give and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN 
ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the sum of........................dollars 


($ ), to be applied to the uses of said Association. 


For Endowment 
I give and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN 
ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the sum of. dollars 
($ ), the same to be added to its regular Endowment Fund 
and the income used for the purpose of said Association. 


A Residuary Bequest—For Endowment 


All the rest, residue and remainder of my estate, real and 


personal, I give, devise and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S 
CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the _ interest 


of this fund to be applied to the uses of said Association. 


Where il is desired thal funds be used for a given Branch, it is suggested that 
the following clause be added to any of the suggested forms: preferabiy for the use of

As the formalities in making a Will or a Codicil to a Will must 
be most carefully observed, we advise that in such cases one’s 


attorney be consulted.
